lesson.title: Breaking Down: One Substance Becomes Many
lesson.summary: A decomposition reaction breaks a single compound apart into two or more simpler substances, the structural reverse of a synthesis reaction, following the pattern AB forms A plus B.
lesson.body:
Decomposition reactions are the mirror image of the Synthesis Reactions covered in the previous chapter, and recognizing that relationship is the fastest way to remember the pattern. Where synthesis combines simple substances into one complex product, decomposition starts with a single compound and breaks it apart into two or more simpler substances, following the general form AB -> A + B. Both patterns belong to the same family introduced back in Reaction Types Overview, just running in opposite directions.

Because decomposition means taking apart bonds that were holding a stable compound together, these reactions typically need an input of energy to get going, commonly supplied as heat, electricity, or light, rather than releasing energy the way many synthesis reactions do. A widely used real-world example is the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, the primary mineral in limestone. When heated strongly in a kiln, calcium carbonate breaks down into calcium oxide, commonly known as quicklime, and carbon dioxide gas. This single reaction is the chemical basis of an enormous industry: quicklime is a key raw material in cement production and in numerous other construction and chemical processes.

Written with state symbols, the reaction is CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g). Checking the balance: the left side has 1 calcium atom, 1 carbon atom, and 3 oxygen atoms, all from the single formula unit of CaCO3. The right side has CaO, contributing 1 calcium atom and 1 oxygen atom, plus CO2, contributing 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms; adding the oxygen from both products gives 1 plus 2 = 3. Both sides show 1 Ca, 1 C, and 3 O, so the equation is balanced, and notice that every coefficient here is an implied 1. This is a useful reminder from Balancing Equations that a correctly balanced equation does not always require large coefficients; sometimes the formulas themselves already account for every atom without any adjustment at all.

Other decomposition reactions follow the same basic shape even though the details differ. Running an electric current through water splits it into hydrogen and oxygen gas, 2 H2O -> 2 H2 + O2, which is simply the reverse of the synthesis reaction that formed water in the first place. Hydrogen peroxide, H2O2, slowly decomposes into water and oxygen gas even at room temperature, which is why hydrogen peroxide bottles are stored away from light and eventually need replacing. In every case, the underlying pattern is the same: one compound in, two or more simpler substances out.
